title: A Junk-Removal Truck Was Reported Outside Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump’s Home
description_medium: A passerby reported seeing a College Hunks Hauling Junk truck outside Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump’s Washington home in January 2021. The company offered both moving and junk-removal services, so the vehicle alone does not establish what crew members were doing. No public business or government activity is identified in the account.
description_long: The record concerns a reported vehicle sighting at the couple’s private residence during the final days of the first Trump administration. A passerby identified the truck as belonging to College Hunks Hauling Junk, a firm that also offers moving services. The photograph’s date, what the crew handled, and whether it performed any service remain unknown. Nothing in the reported incident connects the visit to Jared Kushner’s former White House position, Ivanka Trump’s public role, or government resources. The sighting describes activity at a private home; it does not indicate any policy decision or official action.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: Jared and Ivanka have ‘junk’ removed from Washington, D.C. home
corrected_wording.corrected_title: A Junk-Removal Truck Was Reported Outside Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump’s Home
corrected_wording.reason: The evidence establishes a reported truck sighting, not that junk was removed.

source_access_notes: The TrumpFile timeline and the linked social-media post are the sources for the reported sighting; the New York Times link concerns January 6 and does not corroborate it.
blockers: The available account identifies a truck outside the residence but does not establish when the image was taken, what service the crew performed, or any connection to government business.
rationale: Keeps a mundane household sighting separate from the unsupported claim that items were removed or public business was involved.

title: Donald Trump Jr. Endorses Calls for Shareholder Activism at Big Companies
description_medium: On January 9, 2021, Donald Trump Jr. shared Fox host Laura Ingraham’s call for Republicans to attend large-company shareholder meetings and question executives about alleged discrimination against conservative customers. His post reached about 6.5 million followers. The proposed action was shareholder questioning, not physically entering or taking over company offices.
description_long: Donald Trump Jr. amplified a post by Fox host Laura Ingraham urging Republicans to attend shareholder meetings of large companies and ask why, in her view, those businesses discriminated against Republican customers. Trump Jr. shared the message on January 9, 2021, to an audience reported at 6.5 million followers. The call came amid a dispute between conservatives and technology companies over content moderation and claims of political bias. Shareholder meetings are formal corporate forums where investors can raise questions and vote on certain matters; attending one is different from occupying or forcibly entering a company’s premises. The post did not name a target company or document a resulting meeting, coordinated campaign, or change in corporate policy. Its headline phrase “storm big tech companies” overstates the tactic described in Ingraham’s message and risks implying physical action that the post did not call for.

corrected_wording.original_title: Donald Trump Jr. wants followers to storm big tech companies next
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Donald Trump Jr. Endorses Calls for Shareholder Activism at Big Companies
corrected_wording.reason: The linked call concerned shareholder meetings and questions, not physically storming company offices.

source_access_notes: The supplied TrumpFile timeline page was reviewed; it reproduces the shareholder-meeting language and Trump Jr.’s response.
rationale: Corrects “storm” to the proposed shareholder-meeting questions and distinguishes political advocacy from physical action.

title: Trump releases video condemning violence and ‘censorship'
description_medium: On January 13, 2021, hours after the House voted to impeach him for a second time, Donald Trump released a video condemning the violence at the Capitol and urging against further violence. He also objected to what he called censorship after social-media companies suspended his accounts. The video condemned the attack but did not concede his election loss.
description_long: Donald Trump released a prerecorded video on January 13, 2021, the day the House impeached him for a second time over the January 6 attack on the Capitol. In it, he said he condemned the violence and told supporters that violence was never an acceptable response. He also said that people who engaged in violence would face the law. Alongside that condemnation, Trump criticized social-media companies for suspending his accounts, calling the removals censorship and arguing that free speech was under attack. The combination drew attention because the speech addressed the Capitol attack while also challenging the platforms’ response to his election-related posts. Trump did not concede that he had lost the 2020 election. The video was a public statement during the transition, not a change in the election result or a reversal of the companies’ moderation decisions. His accounts remained suspended as the video was released.
source_access_notes: PBS NewsHour’s contemporaneous report and the TrumpFile timeline were used for the video’s timing and reported themes.
rationale: Places the video after the second impeachment vote and separates the violence condemnation from Trump’s criticism of platform suspensions.

title: Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller Orders Michael Ellis Installed as NSA General Counsel
description_medium: Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller ordered the National Security Agency to install Michael Ellis as its general counsel in January 2021, days before the presidential transition. Ellis took the post on January 19. NSA Director Paul Nakasone placed him on administrative leave the next day while the Defense Department inspector general examined the selection process.
description_long: Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller directed NSA Director Paul Nakasone to install Michael Ellis as the agency’s general counsel in the final days of the Trump administration. Ellis had worked as a White House national-security official and previously served as counsel to Representative Devin Nunes. The general counsel position was a career civilian job at the intelligence agency. After Miller pressed for the appointment, the NSA said it would proceed, and Ellis took the position on January 19, 2021. Nakasone placed him on administrative leave the following day while the Defense Department inspector general examined the circumstances of his selection. The timing, immediately before the change in administrations, prompted objections from lawmakers and former officials. The reporting attributes the directive to Miller; it does not establish that Trump personally ordered Ellis’s installation or that Ellis changed NSA operations before being placed on leave.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump's DoD orders the NSA to immediately install Michael Ellis as top lawyer
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller Orders Michael Ellis Installed as NSA General Counsel
corrected_wording.reason: The supplied reporting attributes the order to Miller, not to Trump personally.

source_access_notes: The Washington Post and CBS News reports provide the appointment, installation, and administrative-leave sequence.
rationale: Attributes the installation order to Christopher Miller and reports Ellis’s installation and leave in sequence.

title: Russian Anti-Corruption Foundation Asks Biden to Sanction 35 Russians
description_medium: In January 2021, Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation asked President Joe Biden to sanction 35 Russian officials and business figures it associated with corruption, repression, and Navalny’s persecution. The foundation highlighted eight people as priorities; seven of the 35 were already under U.S. sanctions. This was an advocacy request to the Biden administration, not a Trump action.
description_long: Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation sent the Biden administration a list of 35 Russian officials and business figures it wanted sanctioned. The request followed Navalny’s return to Russia on January 17, 2021, and his subsequent detention. The foundation said the people on its list were connected to corruption, suppression of civil and political freedoms, or the persecution of Navalny and his organization. It identified eight names as a priority shortlist; seven of the full 35 were already subject to U.S. sanctions. The request was directed to President Joe Biden after he took office and asked for new executive action. It was not itself a sanctions decision, and the description should preserve the foundation’s allegations as allegations. Although the event appears in a Trump-focused timeline, the supplied record establishes no direct connection to Trump beyond cross-references to people mentioned elsewhere in that timeline.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: Anti-Corruption Foundation asks Biden to sanction 35 Russians
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Russian Anti-Corruption Foundation Asks Biden to Sanction 35 Russians
corrected_wording.reason: This was an advocacy request to the Biden administration, with no established direct Trump action.

source_access_notes: The supplied timeline attributes the allegations to Navalny’s foundation; CNN coverage is linked in the record for the request.
blockers: This January 2021 advocacy request was directed to President Biden; the supplied evidence establishes no direct Trump action or connection beyond cross-references to other timeline entries.
rationale: Describes the foundation’s Biden-era sanctions request and makes clear the record does not document a Trump action.

title: Trump: Ted Cruz, Lindsey Graham, and Mike Lee meet with Trump lawyers
description_medium: On February 11, 2021, Senators Ted Cruz, Lindsey Graham, and Mike Lee met privately with Donald Trump’s impeachment lawyers during the Senate trial. The meeting took place as the defense prepared to present its case. David Schoen described it as a discussion of procedure, while Cruz said the senators also discussed legal strategy and the trial’s standard for incitement.
description_long: During Donald Trump’s second Senate impeachment trial, Republican senators Ted Cruz, Lindsey Graham, and Mike Lee met privately with defense lawyers David Schoen and Bruce Castor on February 11, 2021. The meeting came after House impeachment managers had presented their case and on the eve of the defense presentation. The senators were members of the body that would decide whether to convict Trump. Schoen told reporters that the discussion concerned trial procedure and described the senators as friendly visitors. Cruz later said he had urged the lawyers to focus on the legal standard for incitement and had discussed his views on the case. The accounts differed about the meeting’s scope, but both establish that senators spoke with counsel while the trial was underway. The episode raised questions about the appearance of senators advising a defense team while serving as jurors; the available reporting does not establish an improper agreement or a specific effect on the trial’s outcome.
source_access_notes: Contemporaneous Washington Post reporting describes the meeting and the participants’ differing accounts; the Senate roll-call record documents the trial’s final vote.
rationale: Sets out the senators’ role as jurors and the differing accounts of the discussion without inferring an improper agreement.

title: Donald Trump and Don Jr. tap campaign lawyer Jesse Binnall for Swalwell lawsuit
description_medium: After Representative Eric Swalwell sued Donald Trump, Donald Trump Jr., Rudy Giuliani, and Representative Mo Brooks over their alleged roles in the January 6 attack, Jesse Binnall appeared as counsel for the two Trumps. Binnall had represented Trump’s 2020 campaign in election-related litigation. The suit alleged that the defendants helped incite the attack; those allegations were claims in a civil complaint, not findings at filing.
description_long: Representative Eric Swalwell filed a federal civil lawsuit on March 5, 2021, against Donald Trump, Donald Trump Jr., Rudy Giuliani, and Representative Mo Brooks. The complaint alleged that the defendants’ words and actions helped incite the January 6 attack on the Capitol and violated federal civil-rights law. The defendants disputed the allegations. On March 24, attorney Jesse Binnall filed notices of appearance for both Donald Trump and Donald Trump Jr. in the case. Binnall had represented Trump’s 2020 campaign in litigation challenging election results, placing a familiar campaign lawyer on the defense team for a separate post-election case. The filing established who would represent the two defendants; it did not decide the merits of Swalwell’s allegations. A district court later dismissed Trump Jr. from the suit while allowing some claims against Trump to proceed at that stage, illustrating that the claims were treated defendant by defendant rather than as a single finding against everyone named.
source_access_notes: The federal docket confirms Binnall’s March 24 appearances; contemporaneous reporting and the district court order provide the suit’s allegations and procedural posture.
rationale: Connects Binnall’s court filing to the Swalwell civil complaint and distinguishes allegations from court findings.

title: Trump: New York AG joins Manhattan DA's Trump investigation
description_medium: On May 18, 2021, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced that her office was assisting Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance Jr.’s criminal investigation of the Trump Organization. James’s office had been conducting a separate civil inquiry and said that it was now also investigating the company in a criminal capacity. The announcement described cooperation between the offices, not a finding of guilt.
description_long: New York Attorney General Letitia James announced on May 18, 2021, that her office was assisting Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance Jr.’s criminal investigation of the Trump Organization. The announcement marked a change in the attorney general’s office’s role: it had been conducting a civil investigation, and James said it was now investigating the organization in a criminal capacity alongside the Manhattan DA. The offices were examining the company’s business practices, while the district attorney’s office had already been pursuing a criminal inquiry. The two investigations remained institutionally distinct even as staff cooperated. The announcement did not mean that Donald Trump or the company had been found guilty, and it did not itself announce charges. It was a procedural development in New York’s scrutiny of the organization. James’s office later described its assistance as contributing to a criminal indictment of the company in 2021, but that later outcome should not be conflated with the announcement date or treated as a finding against Trump personally.
source_access_notes: The New York Attorney General’s 2021 review and contemporaneous Guardian reporting confirm the announcement and distinguish the civil inquiry from criminal assistance.
rationale: Clarifies that James’s office began assisting the DA’s criminal probe while its civil inquiry remained a separate process.

title: J.D. Vance Urges Reversal of Federal Protections for Reproductive Health Records
description_medium: In June 2023, Senator J.D. Vance joined Republican colleagues in urging the Biden administration not to adopt a proposed HHS privacy rule restricting disclosures of reproductive-health records to law enforcement. The senators argued that the rule could hinder investigations under state abortion laws. Their letter opposed a privacy protection; it did not establish a system for tracking women seeking abortions.
description_long: Senator J.D. Vance and Republican colleagues wrote to Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra in June 2023 to oppose a proposed privacy rule concerning reproductive-health records. The proposal would limit when covered health providers could disclose information for certain investigations, including inquiries into reproductive care that was lawful where it occurred. The lawmakers argued that the rule exceeded HHS authority and could interfere with enforcement of state abortion restrictions. Their letter asked the administration not to finalize the protection as proposed. It did not create a national pregnancy registry, direct agencies to track women, or describe an operational tracking system. The headline’s description of Vance wanting to “track women seeking abortions” turns opposition to a medical-record privacy rule into a claim about a separate practice. The letter documents Vance’s position on privacy and state enforcement; it does not establish a Trump administration policy or a direct Trump proposal. The letter reflects Vance’s position as a senator before Trump returned to office.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: J.D. Vance wants to track women seeking abortions
corrected_wording.corrected_title: J.D. Vance Urges Reversal of Federal Protections for Reproductive Health Records
corrected_wording.reason: The supplied record describes a letter about privacy protections, not a system to track women seeking abortions.

source_access_notes: HHS explains the reproductive-health privacy rule; Spectrum News reports Vance’s letter and its stated objections.
blockers: The 2023 letter documents Vance’s opposition to a proposed reproductive-record privacy rule, but the supplied evidence does not establish a pregnancy-tracking proposal or a direct Trump action.
rationale: Replaces pregnancy-tracking framing with the documented letter opposing a proposed reproductive-record privacy rule.

title: Hungary’s Viktor Orbán Opposes Ukraine EU Accession Talks at 2023 Summit
description_medium: At the December 2023 European Council summit, Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán publicly opposed opening EU accession talks with Ukraine and had threatened to veto the decision. The leaders ultimately opened talks after Orbán left the room during the vote. The event is a Hungarian policy dispute within the EU, with no documented Trump action.
description_long: The European Council met in Brussels on December 14, 2023, to consider opening EU membership negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova. Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán had publicly opposed starting talks with Ukraine, saying the country was not ready and that the EU should first pursue a strategic partnership. He had threatened to veto the decision, which required unanimity. The leaders ultimately agreed to open negotiations after Orbán left the room during the vote. The decision began a lengthy accession process; it did not make Ukraine an EU member. Orbán’s opposition was part of a broader dispute over EU support for Ukraine and Hungary’s relations with the bloc. Claims that Hungarian and Russian officials coordinated through intercepted communications are not substantiated by the contemporaneous reporting on the summit. The documented event is Orbán’s public position and the Council’s decision, rather than proven covert coordination or a Trump administration action.

corrected_wording.original_title: Trump: Hungarian and Russian officials caught on intercepts coordinating to block Ukraine from EU
corrected_wording.corrected_title: Hungary’s Viktor Orbán Opposes Ukraine EU Accession Talks at 2023 Summit
corrected_wording.reason: Public reporting verifies Orbán’s opposition at the summit; it does not substantiate the alleged intercepts or a Trump connection.

source_access_notes: AP and Reuters contemporaneous reporting document Orbán’s public position and the European Council decision; the intercepted-coordination claim is not independently established there.
blockers: The alleged Hungarian-Russian coordination through intercepted communications is not corroborated by contemporaneous reporting. No direct Trump action or connection is documented.
rationale: Retitle to the documented public dispute over Ukraine accession and avoid presenting the uncorroborated intercept allegation as fact.
